title: The servant's ear (Luke 22:47–53)
hook: even while arrested he heals the ear Peter cut off

segments.voice: Yesterday, agonia: sweat like drops of blood, and an angel who strengthened him. Your line was an angel strengthened him.

The prayer in the garden is over. Torches come up the hill: a crowd with swords and clubs, and at the front a familiar face, Judas, one of the twelve, leaning in to kiss his teacher. In the dark it happens fast. Someone near Jesus asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? and doesn't wait for the answer. A blade swings. The servant of the high priest is holding the side of his head; his right ear is gone. What Jesus does next is the last healing Luke records before the cross.
screen: `TORCHES IN THE GARDEN.` → `A KISS, THEN A SWORD.` → `A RIGHT EAR CUT OFF.`

segments.voice: All four Gospels tell of the sword in the garden. Only John gives the names: the one with the sword is Simon Peter, and the servant is Malchus. Only Luke, the doctor's Gospel by old tradition, tells what happened next: "But Jesus answering, said: Suffer ye thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him." Suffer ye thus far is an old phrase, and nobody is fully sure of the Greek's exact sense. Many modern readers hear no more of this: enough, stop here. Others hear Jesus speaking to the crowd: let me go this far, let me reach him. Either way, the fighting ends with a hand on a stranger's wound. Look who gets healed: not a friend or a disciple, but a man who came out at night to arrest him. And look when: Jesus is about to be bound, and his own hands are still free to touch. Then he tells the chief priests and captains plainly that they could have taken him any day in the temple, "but this is your hour, and the power of darkness." He names the darkness and doesn't fight it with a sword. He refuses violence, and he repairs what his own side broke. Peter swung the blade; Jesus cleans up after Peter. Most of the damage we have to mend wasn't done by our enemies. It was done by us, or by people on our side, trying to help.
screen: `PETER'S SWORD, MALCHUS'S EAR.` · `SUFFER YE THUS FAR.` · `HE HEALS THE MAN WHO CAME FOR HIM.` · `THIS IS YOUR HOUR.` · then, large: `HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that broke because of you: a sharp word in a group chat, a borrowed thing returned worse, a friendship you let go quiet on purpose. Picture what touching it would look like: a message, an apology with no excuse attached, fixing the thing. If you pray, ask for the nerve to mend it; if not, just hold it in front of you and choose one small next step.
Malchus. The name John gives the servant whose ear Peter cut off, and whom Jesus touched and healed while the soldiers closed in. Today's word.
Your line: no more of this. A hand on a wound, right where a fight was starting. That's day four hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the arrest in the garden in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and the healing of the servant's ear is preached by many as Christ's refusal of violence even in his own defense.

chat.says: Did Jesus ever heal someone who was against him?
options: Yes: in the garden he touched the ear of a man who came to arrest him, and healed it.
Yes, but only after the man had first apologized and asked to follow him.
No; in Luke he heals only his own followers and the people who ask him.
chat.meaning: Luke says Jesus touched the ear of the high priest's servant and healed him, a man who came out at night to arrest him.

notes: The carry 'no more of this' is a modern rendering of Luke 22:51 (the Douay and KJV read 'Suffer ye thus far'); the script explains both. Confirm.
'The last healing Luke records before the cross': confirm against Luke 22–23.
Luke as 'the doctor's Gospel by old tradition' rests on Colossians 4:14 and early tradition; confirm phrasing.
Two readings of 'suffer ye thus far' (to the disciples: stop; to the captors: let me reach him) are given without ranking; confirm both are fairly described.
Original: ὠτίον in Luke 22:51 (Luke 22:50 has οὖς); confirm the spelling and verse.
